30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 13: Bringing the Numbers to Life — A Stats Page and Pie Chart with Chart.js
Our expense tracker app pretty much has a working prototype now. There's even a category breakdown in there that shows you which categories you're spending the most on.

But... humans are visual creatures. If the screen looks nice and has charts, that beats showing a pile of numbers. So in this post I'll show you how to build a stats page that brings those boring line-by-line numbers to life.
At the same time, we'll cover how to deal with tech you're not familiar with, like how to choose and set up something like Chart.js.
Ask the AI to recommend a dish
So what do you do when you're facing tech you don't know? Let me use eating at a restaurant as an example.
Say we walk into a restaurant and the menu has a ton of dishes, but we're not sure what to order. So we ask the server to recommend a few. That's exactly what we're doing here too.
When you need to build something you're not familiar with, you can ask the AI to recommend a few options and list the pros and cons, and then you make the final call on which tech to use.
So... how do you do it? Here's an example prompt I put together for you (don't forget to switch to Plan Mode):
language-txt shiki shiki-themes github-light github-light github-dark-high-contrast

I want to build a stats page that shows this month's spending stats:
- Add two tabs to the app: Expenses (the current screen) and Stats.
- The stats page shows this month's total spending, this month's number of entries, and a pie chart of this month's breakdown by category.
- Next to the pie chart, also list the category name, amount, and percentage. The data can't rely on color alone.
- Please pull the stats calculation logic out into pure functions. Don't tie it to the UI or storage.
- Acceptance criteria: after adding an expense and switching to the stats page, the total and the pie chart should both reflect the latest data.

On the tech side, you can read SPEC.md to understand my current project's tech. After reading it, list two or three chart library options commonly used in the Vue ecosystem, with the pros and cons of each. Check the options with me first, and only write the plan after I've decided.
Consideration: this project is small. I want the simplest thing that's good enough. No overkill.

This prompt is a little longer than the past few days. The first half is the feature requirements and acceptance criteria, and only the second half is the ordering:

The reason you have to state all the requirements at once is that once the plan comes out and you approve it, it'll build the whole thing in one go. There won't be a break in the middle for you to add more requirements.
You should see the AI recommend a few mainstream libraries like Chart.js or ECharts:

Even though Chart.js + vue-chartjs isn't the recommended option, I'd still personally pick it. After all, it says right there that it's "the most mainstream in the Vue ecosystem, with the most docs and examples, and pie charts are a built-in type." Its API is simple too, which makes it the best fit for a small project.
At this point, please don't rush to press "Yes, and use auto mode." Read through it properly first!

Whenever there's something you don't understand, feel free to press ESC or ask the AI to explain it in "Tell Claude what to change." That way you'll understand its approach better, which will also help you with future development.
Once you've picked, it'll start writing the plan. Same as before, you don't need to read every word. Just look at a few key points:
Is the library it's using the one you just picked?
Did it pull the "calculation" part out into pure functions like you asked, instead of stuffing everything into the component?
Did SPEC.md get updated too? For example, my SPEC.md originally said not to install a chart library. Now that we've decided to install one, that line needs to change as well.

By the way, my plan also made a decision I didn't ask for: it removed the row of category breakdown bars from the expenses page and moved it to the stats page. Its reasoning was that the same data shouldn't be drawn two different ways, because if you change one, it's easy to forget the other. So when it's done, you'll notice the bars on the home page are gone. Don't assume it broke something. For decisions like this that it adds on its own, approve them if you understand the reasoning, and ask if you don't. Don't just quietly let them through.
If it all looks fine, press
. It'll run the install first (if a permission prompt pops up, give it a quick look before approving), and then build.
One more reminder: package versions are usually the thing the AI's memory is most likely to have out of date. So once it finishes installing, I recommend checking the version numbers in
to make sure they're the latest, or the version you want.
Then you'll see it create two pieces:
A file that handles the "calculating" (for me it's
A chart component that handles the "drawing" (

Your file names might not be exactly the same as mine, but you don't need to understand the code. Just know how the work is split: the first one only calculates "how much was spent in each category and what share each one takes." It takes data in and spits numbers out, and doesn't care about the screen at all. The second one takes those numbers and draws the pie chart.
If you want to check that it did this, just open the project folder and see whether two similar files showed up.
If you're really curious what's going on inside, just ask it "Explain in plain language what stats.js does." That's way faster than forcing yourself to read the code.
Review: does the chart move with the data?
Next, of course, we need to review the result. Seeing the screen below doesn't mean it passed:
The stats page's pie chart of this month's spending by category
So how do we actually review this? First, let's clear out the practice data from before:
Open the developer tools (F12, or Cmd+Option+I on macOS)
Switch to the Application tab, and under Local Storage on the left, find your URL (normally
The screen should be empty now. Next, let's add some test data:
This month's total is 200, with 2 entries
Last month's 999 isn't counted at all
Pie chart of this month's spending by category
Once that checks out, go back to the expenses page and add one more entry, "Entertainment 200 for this month," then switch back to the stats page. This time, we expect:
This month's total is 400, with 3 entries
The pie chart changing after adding another expense
And with that, we've finished Week 2's core MVP. Don't forget to have the AI commit.
So the stats page is done too. Let's wrap up with a quick summary:

When you run into tech you don't know, ask the AI to recommend a dish: give it your requirements and constraints, have it list options with pros and cons, and only say yes once you understand the reasoning. You don't have to pick the one it marked as recommended.

Once you approve a Plan Mode plan, it builds the whole thing in one go, so state all your requirements at once. For decisions it adds to the plan on its own, approve them if you understand the reasoning, and ask if you don't.
After installing packages, take a look at the versions in
Review by the numbers, not the chart: use a fixed set of entries, work out the expected values ahead of time, and compare. The chart looking like "it kind of changed" doesn't count.
As of today, all the core features in SPEC.md are in place, and this expense tracker app is basically a usable MVP.
